posts.headline: The Fed is now expected to raise rates, not cut them
posts.caption:
For most of this year the question was when the Fed would cut. That question is gone.

After yesterday's inflation report, futures markets put the odds of a rate increase at the December 9 meeting at about 89%. A week ago it was roughly 72%. Markets are no longer pricing in any chance of the Fed simply holding.

The target range today is 3.75% to 4.00%.

My take: a cut helps borrowers and an increase helps savers. For the first time in a while, the people with cash are the ones being paid to wait.

Which side of that are you on right now?

Source: CME FedWatch, Nov 10 2026
Educational only — not financial advice.

posts.headline: Banks are closed today. Your money still moves, mostly
posts.caption:
Today is Veterans Day, a federal holiday. Here is what that actually changes.

Bank branches are shut and there is no mail. The bond market is closed. The stock market is open and trading normally.

The part that catches people: a transfer or a bill payment you start today will not settle today. It picks up tomorrow. If something is due today, it may land late through no fault of yours.

My take: check anything dated today before you go to bed, not after the late fee.

Anything due today you should go and look at?

posts.headline: The December meeting in three numbers
posts.caption:
Three numbers worth carrying into December.

The federal funds target range sits at 3.75% to 4.00% today. The committee meets on December 8 and 9. Futures markets put the chance of an increase at that meeting near 89%.

Nothing is decided. The Fed sees another jobs report before it votes.

My take: 89% is not certainty, but it is the market telling you which way to lean.

Are you planning around a higher rate or a lower one?

Source: Federal Reserve, Oct 28 2026 statement · CME FedWatch

posts.headline: Two people inside the Fed already voted to raise rates
posts.caption:
The Fed held rates steady on October 28. The vote was not unanimous.

Two governors, Lisa Cook and Beth Hammack, dissented. Both wanted a quarter-point increase that day. That was before the inflation figures that landed this week.

Dissents are rare and they are public on purpose. They are the clearest signal you get about where the next decision is heading.

My take: when two of them wanted to move early and the data since has been hotter, December starts to look less like a question.

Did you know the Fed publishes who disagreed?

Source: Federal Reserve, Oct 28 2026 statement

posts.headline: Mortgage rates are falling. They are also far above last year
posts.caption:
Both of these are true at the same time, and only one of them makes the headline.

The 30-year fixed averaged 7.18% in the week to November 5. That is down from 7.24% the week before, a third straight weekly fall.

A year ago the same average was 6.22%.

So rates are falling, and a buyer today still borrows at nearly a full point more than a buyer last November.

My take: direction and level are different questions. Headlines report direction. You pay the level.

Which number would change your plans?

Source: Freddie Mac PMMS, Nov 5 2026

posts.headline: What a rate rise actually reaches in your life
posts.source: Source: how Fed policy transmits to consumer rates
posts.caption:
The Fed does not set your credit card rate. It sets the rate banks lend to each other overnight, and almost everything else drifts after it.

Card APRs move fastest. Most are variable and tied to the prime rate, so a Fed increase usually shows up on your statement within a billing cycle or two.

Savings rates move next, but only if your bank feels like competing for your deposit. Many do not.

Mortgages follow the bond market rather than the Fed directly, so they can move early, late, or the other way entirely.

My take: a hike lands on your debt quickly and on your savings slowly. That gap is where banks make money.

Which of yours would move first?

Source: how Fed policy transmits to consumer rates

posts.headline: What a card charges when you carry a balance
posts.caption:
The Federal Reserve tracks what Americans actually pay on cards, not what the advert says.

For accounts carrying interest, the average rate was 22.36% in August 2026.

Carry $3,000 at that rate and the interest alone is about $56 in the first month. Pay $100 and roughly half of it never touches what you owe.

That is the part people miss. The minimum payment is mostly rent on the balance.

My take: anything above about 20% is an emergency, not a bill.

Do you know the rate on the card in your pocket?

Source: Federal Reserve G.19, August 2026
Educational only — not financial advice.

posts.headline: The same $10,000. Four different rates
posts.caption:
Same money in, same twenty years, nothing added. Only the rate changes.

At 2% a year, $10,000 becomes about $14,900.
At 4%, about $21,900.
At 7%, about $38,700.
At 10%, about $67,300.

There is a shortcut for thinking about this. Divide 72 by the rate and you get roughly the years it takes to double. At 2% that is 36 years. At 10% it is about 7.

My take: the gap between the top and bottom bar is not the rate. It is time multiplied by the rate, and that is why starting early beats picking well.

What rate is your money sitting at right now?

Source: calculated over 20 years

posts.headline: An emergency fund covers your bills, not your salary
posts.caption:
People hear six months of savings and quietly give up. Usually because they are doing the wrong sum.

It is six months of expenses, not six months of income. If you earn $5,000 a month and live on $3,200, the target is built on the $3,200.

And expenses in an emergency are not normal expenses. No holidays, no subscriptions you would cancel, no dinners out. The real number is often smaller again.

My take: work out what one bad month actually costs before you decide the goal is impossible.

Do you know what one month of your essentials costs?

Source: standard emergency fund guidance

posts.headline: What $300 a month looks like after a year
posts.caption:
Nothing dramatic. That is rather the point.

Put aside $300 a month in an account paying 4%, add nothing else, and after twelve months you have about $3,670. After seventeen months you cross $5,000.

The interest in that first year is around $70. Almost all of it is simply the money you put in.

My take: at this stage the rate barely matters. Showing up every month is doing all the work. The rate starts to matter later, once there is something for it to work on.
